passage: You asked how it felt, turning fourteen. Okay. I'm Pranav. That year I grew fast, and my arms got long and thin and my voice cracked. My cousin Leela, she's older, showed me photos of some boys online with huge muscles. I started comparing everything. I'd stand sideways in the mirror. I skipped dinner a few times, thinking it would make me look sharper. Then Leela noticed, and she felt terrible, I think. She sat with me and said those photos are edited, posed, lit perfectly. She said my body was still changing and would do its own thing. Our PE teacher said the same, and that if I was worried I could talk to the doctor. I stopped skipping meals. I still stand sideways sometimes. But I laugh at myself now.

qa.q: What did Pranav skip a few times?
qa.a: Pranav skipped dinner a few times.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she noticed Pranav skipping meals?
qa.a: Pranav thinks she felt terrible, likely because the photos she had shown Pranav seemed to have started his comparing.

qa.q: What made the adults' and Leela's responses helpful?
qa.a: They explained that the photos were edited and posed, reminded Pranav that a growing body keeps changing, and pointed him to a doctor if worried, without shaming.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had never noticed?
qa.a: Pranav might have kept skipping meals and comparing himself to edited images, and the harmful habit could have grown quietly.

grounding: A teen describes comparing a changing body to idealised images, starting a harmful habit, and turning towards acceptance with support.

passage: I'm Mridul. Ojas and I have been in the same swimming class since Class 7. This year he started wearing a big T-shirt over his swimsuit, even in the water. Coach asked him to take it off, and Ojas went red and said he was cold. He wasn't. He'd been quiet in the changing room since some older boys joked about the hair on his chest. After that he missed two classes. I didn't really know what to say, so I told him that my shoulders are crooked and I've stopped caring. He laughed a little. Last week he came without the T-shirt. He still turned his back when the older boys walked by. Coach told them off for teasing and changed the lane groups.

qa.q: What did Ojas start wearing over his swimsuit?
qa.a: He started wearing a big T-shirt.

qa.q: Why did Ojas say he was cold when he wasn't?
qa.a: He was embarrassed about his body after the older boys' jokes and needed an excuse to keep covered without explaining.

qa.q: How did the coach help, and what else could Coach do?
qa.a: Coach stopped the teasing and changed lane groups; Coach could also have a private word with Ojas to check how he's feeling.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul to watch this happen?
qa.a: Mridul seems unsure what to say and a bit worried, so shares a personal insecurity to make Ojas feel less alone.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen hiding his changing body after teasing, and gradually regaining some self-acceptance.

passage:
Week one: Urmila deleted her class photo from her profile because her face looked "round." Her friend Kashish commented, "You look nice!" Urmila didn't believe her. She spent the evening comparing herself with a filtered model's pictures.

Week three: In health class, the teacher showed how one photo can be changed with filters and lighting. Urmila felt oddly angry at how much time she'd wasted. She unfollowed several accounts that made her feel worse.

Week six: She and Kashish went cycling on Sunday and laughed so much she forgot about her face. At home she noticed she hadn't opened the mirror app in days. She reposted the class photo. It still felt strange, but she kept it up. 🙂

qa.q: What did the health teacher show the class in week three?
qa.a: The teacher showed how one photo can be changed with filters and lighting.

qa.q: Why did Urmila feel angry after the health class?
qa.a: She realised she had been comparing herself to images that weren't real, and felt upset about the time she had wasted feeling bad.

qa.q: What choices helped Urmila move towards self-acceptance?
qa.a: Unfollowing accounts that made her feel worse and spending time on active fun with Kashish shifted her focus away from her looks.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Urmila didn't believe her compliment?
qa.a: She might have felt sad or powerless, since her kind words couldn't reach her friend at that moment.

grounding: It shows a teen moving over several weeks from comparing herself to filtered images towards accepting her own appearance.

passage: Irfan, you've been skipping dinner and doing push-ups at midnight, I've seen. Sit, let me tell you something. At sixteen I had a poster of an action hero on my wall, all muscles. I looked at my thin arms in the mirror every morning and felt like a joke. So I started skipping meals and running in the heat, thinking I'd get that shape faster. At football practice one day, everything went white and I sat down hard on the ground. Coach Dsouza called my father, and we went to the doctor. The doctor said my body was still growing and needed fuel. Coach told me, 'That poster has lights and makeup and a team behind it.' I started eating properly and training slowly. Talk to me before you copy some poster, hah?

qa.q: What happened to the narrator at football practice?
qa.a: Everything went white and the narrator sat down hard on the ground.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel as a teen looking in the mirror?
qa.a: The narrator felt inadequate and embarrassed, like a joke, comparing their thin arms with the muscular hero on the poster.

qa.q: Why does the narrator ask Irfan to talk to them?
qa.a: The narrator has seen Irfan skipping dinner and training at midnight, and wants Irfan to get support before harming their health.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel hearing that the narrator went through the same thing?
qa.a: Irfan might feel less alone and more open to changing those habits without feeling judged. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls teenage body comparison and harmful habits, and a healthier path with trusted adults.

passage: Swimming class started in twenty minutes, and the changing room was loud, steamy and crowded. Darshan, fifteen, stood in the corner with his T-shirt still on. He'd grown softer around the middle this year, and the boys in the reels he scrolled all looked carved from stone. He thought about pretending to have a cold. Madhav, already in his trunks, flicked water at him. 'You coming or what?' 'Maybe I'll sit this one out.' Madhav looked at him properly. 'Dude, half those guys online have filters. You beat me in freestyle last month.' Darshan remembered that race, the burn in his arms, the fun of it. He pulled off the T-shirt quickly before he could change his mind. In the water, he forgot about it.

qa.q: How long was it until swimming class started?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Darshan think about pretending to have a cold?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious about his body compared with the boys in the reels and wanted to avoid being seen.

qa.q: What helped Darshan choose to swim?
qa.a: Madhav reminded him that online images are filtered and that his body could win races, so he focused on what it can do.

qa.q: What might Madhav have noticed that made him look at Darshan properly?
qa.a: He probably noticed Darshan hesitating in his T-shirt and sensed something was wrong beyond laziness.

grounding: Shows a teen handling body comparison with idealised images and choosing a healthy activity.

passage:
Sunaina, fifteen, scrolled through photos of girls with perfect skin and tiny waists on the bus home in Mumbai. She pinched her own stomach and frowned.
For a week, she skipped her lunch at school and told her mother she'd eaten.
Her brother Yash noticed her tiffin coming home full. “Didi, you're not eating?”
“Don't tell Mummy.”
But that night he did. Their mother came and sat on Sunaina's bed. She didn't shout. “Beta, those photos are edited. You're growing. Your body needs food to grow.”
Sunaina cried a little. Together they unfollowed a dozen accounts. The next day, her mother booked a chat with the school counsellor, and Sunaina ate her whole tiffin.

qa.q: How did Yash notice Sunaina wasn't eating?
qa.a: He noticed her tiffin coming home full.

qa.q: How was Sunaina feeling about her body?
qa.a: She felt insecure and unhappy, comparing herself to edited photos.

qa.q: What did her mother do that helped, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She stayed calm, explained the photos are edited and that growing bodies need food, helped unfollow accounts and involved the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt telling his mother despite Sunaina's request?
qa.a: He probably felt worried and torn, but knew telling a trusted adult was right.

grounding: A fifteen-year-old caught in comparison is helped by her family to stop a harmful habit.

passage:
“Ganga, look at this guy's arms.” Abhinav held up his phone at the school gate.
“So?”
“Mine look like sticks. There's a guy at the gym selling a powder. Says it'll make me big in a month.”
Ganga frowned. “What's in it?”
“No idea. Doesn't matter.”
“It does. Remember that boy in 12th who got sick from some powder? Ask Coach first. Or the doctor.”
Abhinav sighed. “You sound like my mum.”
“Also, half those photos are edited. The lighting, the angle. Nobody looks like that all day.”
“You think?”
“I know. My cousin edits photos for a job.”
Abhinav put his phone away. “Okay. I'll ask Coach tomorrow.”

qa.q: Who did Ganga tell Abhinav to ask first?
qa.a: Coach, or the doctor.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel about his arms?
qa.a: He felt insecure and unhappy, thinking they looked like sticks.

qa.q: What did Ganga say that helped Abhinav avoid a harmful choice?
qa.a: She warned him about unknown powders, told him to ask Coach or the doctor, and explained that the photos are edited.

qa.q: How might Coach respond when Abhinav asks?
qa.a: Coach will likely be glad he asked and help him with safe training.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old helps a friend resist a risky shortcut born of body comparison.

passage:
At fifteen, my face broke out so badly I stopped going to family photos. I'm Yogesh. I'd stand behind the camera and say I didn't feel like it.
Every morning I checked the mirror and felt sick. I tried every paste and scrub my friends mentioned. It got worse.
My sister Vidya noticed. She didn't say “it's nothing.” She said, “It's not your fault, and you don't have to hide.” Then she told Amma, and Amma took me to a skin doctor.
The doctor was kind, and said it would take time. It did. My skin is better now, not perfect.
Last Diwali, I stood in the family photo. Vidya squeezed my shoulder right as the camera clicked.

qa.q: Who took Yogesh to the skin doctor?
qa.a: Amma took Yogesh to a skin doctor.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about the acne at fifteen?
qa.a: Yogesh felt ashamed and self-conscious, avoiding family photos.

qa.q: What helped Yogesh most, and why?
qa.a: Vidya's kindness and telling Amma, which led to a skin doctor's care instead of trying random products.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when Yogesh joins the Diwali photo?
qa.a: Vidya probably feels happy and proud of Yogesh's courage.

grounding: A teenager overcomes shame about acne with family support and self-acceptance.

passage:
PE teacher's note, Class 9.
For two weeks, Rajni has been skipping lunch and saying she's "not hungry". Today she nearly fainted during the relay. When I asked her friend Priyanka quietly, she said Rajni has been following an influencer's "slim challenge" and comparing herself to edited photos.
I sat with Rajni in the sick room. I told her I was worried about her, not about her shape, and that her body needs food to grow and run. She cried and said she hates how she looks in photos.
I told her it's not her fault that those images are edited to look impossible. With her permission, I called her mother and the school counsellor this afternoon. The counsellor will meet her tomorrow morning. — Salma Ansari

qa.q: What did Rajni nearly do during the relay?
qa.a: She nearly fainted.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when she cried in the sick room?
qa.a: Rajni felt sad and ashamed about how she looks in photos, comparing herself to edited images.

qa.q: What did Salma Ansari do that was right?
qa.a: She focused on Rajni's health, not her shape, explained the edited images, and brought in her mother and the counsellor the same day.

qa.q: How might Priyanka feel after telling the teacher?
qa.a: Priyanka may feel worried but relieved that an adult is now helping her friend.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teen skipping meals due to comparison, and the adult's same-day response.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today I posted a selfie with the filter that makes your face thinner and your skin smooth. It got loads of likes.
Then I looked in the mirror without it. I felt ugly. My real face has a bump on my nose and spots on my chin.
Saurabh, my brother, saw me staring. He said, "You know half those accounts are filtered too, right? It's not real."
"But everyone looks like that."
"Everyone looks like that on their phone. In real life, look at your friends. They have spots. You laugh at the same jokes with them."
I thought about Sonu, who has the best laugh and the worst acne. I love her.
I'm deleting the filter. Maybe I'll just post my dog.
— Lakshmi

qa.q: What did the filter do to Lakshmi's face?
qa.a: Made the face thinner and the skin smooth.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when looking in the mirror without the filter?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt ugly and unhappy, comparing her real face to the filtered one.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi see things differently?
qa.a: Saurabh pointed out filters aren't real, and thinking of a friend Lakshmi loves despite the acne showed that looks aren't what matters.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see filtered photos?
qa.a: Saurabh sees them as not real, a phone version of people, not how anyone really looks.

grounding: In a diary a teen compares their own face to filtered images and finds a healthier view.

passage:
After the wedding season in their small town, Zeenat started comparing herself to a video star whose skin and waist looked perfect in every clip. She began leaving half her lunch, saying she wasn't hungry.
Her cousin Farida, a year older, noticed. One afternoon on the roof, she showed Zeenat a trick: the same photo of herself, with and without a filter. "See? Smoother skin, thinner face. It's the app, not me."
Zeenat laughed a little, then went quiet. "But she's like that in every video."
"Every video has the filter," Farida said. "And you're growing. Growing needs food."
That night Farida sat with Zeenat while she told Ammi about the lunches. Ammi didn't scold. She hugged her, and said they'd see the doctor together if Zeenat kept feeling bad about eating.

qa.q: What did Farida show Zeenat on the roof?
qa.a: The same photo of herself, with and without a filter.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat go quiet after laughing?
qa.a: Zeenat still felt insecure and doubtful, comparing herself to the star who looked perfect in every video.

qa.q: What was the most important step Farida took, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Zeenat while she told Ammi mattered most, because skipping food is a real problem that needs a trusted adult involved.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt hearing about the lunches?
qa.a: Ammi was probably worried but chose to be calm and loving, so Zeenat would keep talking to her.

grounding: Shows a teen affected by idealised filtered images starting to skip food, and family helping her toward self-acceptance and adult support.

passage:
In Brno, the swim class changing room was where Jana felt worst. Her body had changed fast over the summer, and she kept her towel wrapped round her even while changing. She was sure everyone was looking.
One Wednesday, Sofia, from the next bench, said quietly, "I hate this room too. I change in the toilet cubicle sometimes."
Jana stared. Sofia was the fastest swimmer in the group.
"Seriously?"
"Everyone's weird about their body right now. We're all changing."
Jana thought about that in the water. Her legs were strong; her times were good. The coach said her turns were the best in the class.
It didn't disappear. But the next week she didn't wrap the towel quite so tight, and she and Sofia raced the last length laughing.

qa.q: Where does Sofia sometimes change?
qa.a: Sofia sometimes changes in the toilet cubicle.

qa.q: Why did Jana stare when Sofia admitted hating the room too?
qa.a: Jana felt surprised, and a bit relieved, because she had assumed only she felt self-conscious.

qa.q: How could the coach help students who feel like Jana?
qa.a: The coach could offer private changing spaces and praise what bodies can do, like strong legs and good turns, not how they look.

qa.q: What is it like for Sofia to admit those feelings?
qa.a: It probably felt vulnerable for Sofia, but Sofia may have felt less alone once Jana responded.

grounding: Illustrates a teen feeling self-conscious about body changes and moving toward acceptance through a peer's honesty.

passage:
At the sports hostel, Trisha's arms had grown strong from two years of wrestling. One evening in the mess, a few boys from the hockey team flexed and called her "Bhim". Everyone laughed.
That night she stood in front of the mirror, wondering whether to stop training so hard.
Next morning her coach, Kavitha Ma'am, noticed her half-hearted warm-up. "What's going on?"
Trisha told her. Kavitha Ma'am didn't laugh. "Your arms are how you won the district final. They're doing their job. Do you want to be judged for how they look or for what they can do?"
Trisha thought for a long time. Then she tied her hair and went back to the mat.
That week Kavitha Ma'am spoke to the hockey coach, and the teasing stopped.

qa.q: What did the hockey boys call Trisha?
qa.a: They called her "Bhim".

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling in front of the mirror that night?
qa.a: Trisha felt hurt and self-conscious about her strong arms, enough to consider training less.

qa.q: Which of Kavitha Ma'am's actions helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether Trisha wanted to be judged for looks or ability helped her see her strength, and speaking to the hockey coach stopped the teasing.

qa.q: How might the hockey boys see it after their coach speaks to them?
qa.a: They may feel a bit embarrassed and realise the joke hurt a teammate who trains as hard as they do.

grounding: Shows a teen athlete handling teasing about her body and choosing to value what it can do over how it looks.

passage:
Dear Anjali Didi,
You're the only one I can tell this to without being teased.
For months I've been watching gym videos every night. Guys my age with huge arms, perfect abs. I started skipping Ammi's rotis and doing push-ups till my wrists hurt. Last week a boy at the gym offered me a powder "to grow fast" and said not to tell my parents.
I didn't buy it. But I wanted to.
Then I remembered what you said when you were sixteen and stopped eating lunch: "Those photos aren't real life." You looked so tired that year.
So I'm going to talk to Coach about a proper training plan and ask Ammi to take me to the doctor before I try anything. And I'm eating the rotis again.
I still don't like my arms. But maybe I can like them a bit more later.
Wasim

qa.q: What did the boy at the gym offer Wasim?
qa.a: The boy offered a powder "to grow fast".

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when the boy offered the powder?
qa.a: Wasim felt tempted and insecure about body image, even though something about it felt wrong.

qa.q: What wise steps is Wasim taking now?
qa.a: Wasim is talking to Coach about a proper plan, asking Ammi for a doctor visit before trying anything, and eating meals again.

qa.q: How might Anjali Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Anjali would probably feel touched that her old words helped, and relieved that Wasim reached out before trying the powder.

grounding: Shows a teenager struggling with idealised body images but choosing safe, supported habits over harmful ones.
